title: Rebalancing Nature’s Books
gist: Kharas, McCarthy and Sato argue the Kunming-Montreal biodiversity framework is faltering—fewer than half of targets on track for 2030—because the global financial system pays $30 to destroy nature for every $1 invested in it; they urge reframing nature as a bioeconomy growth investment, fixing debt/ratings incentives, supply-chain financing and targeting environmental-crime chokepoints.

insights.claim: The first assessment of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the State of Biodiversity Action report released at COP17 in Yerevan in October 2026, found fewer than half of assessed targets on track for 2030 even though nearly 90% of countries have set targets.
insights.speaker: HOMI KHARAS
insights.so_what: Biodiversity policy pressure likely to intensify, raising regulatory risk for nature-intensive sectors.
insights.quote: fewer than half of the assessed targets are on track to be met by 2030

insights.claim: The authors argue the Kunming-Montreal framework is faltering not because governments are indifferent to nature but because global economic and financial systems reward nature's destruction and penalize its protection.
insights.speaker: HOMI KHARAS
insights.so_what: Expect policy to target financial flows and subsidies rather than just add targets.
insights.quote: global economic and financial systems reward nature’s destruction and penalize its protection

themes.theme: Finance flows and the biodiversity gap

insights.claim: According to UNEP, $7.3 trillion—about 7% of world GDP—flowed into activities that directly harm nature in 2023, meaning $30 was spent destroying nature for every $1 invested in it.
insights.speaker: HOMI KHARAS
insights.so_what: Large nature-harming flows are a target for future subsidy reform and disclosure rules.
insights.quote: For every dollar invested in nature that year, $30 was spent destroying it.

insights.claim: The biodiversity finance gap is $700 billion annually, which the Kunming-Montreal framework seeks to close by cutting nature-harming subsidies by $500 billion a year and mobilizing $200 billion a year in new finance, including $30 billion from external official sources.
insights.speaker: HOMI KHARAS
insights.so_what: Subsidy cuts of $500bn/yr would hit agriculture, fisheries and fossil-linked sectors.

insights.claim: Well over half of the needed biodiversity investment is for sustainable management of farmland, rangeland, fisheries and forests, with the remainder for ecosystem restoration and preservation.
insights.speaker: HOMI KHARAS
insights.so_what: Sustainable agriculture and land-management is the largest addressable segment of nature finance.

insights.claim: Around 55% of global GDP—about $58 trillion—directly depends on nature.
insights.speaker: HOMI KHARAS
insights.so_what: Nature-related risk is systemic for a majority of economic output.
insights.quote: Around 55% of global GDP—equivalent to $58 trillion—already depends directly on nature.

insights.claim: The bioeconomy is worth about $4 trillion today and could grow to $30 trillion by 2050 if its potential is unlocked, linking producers to higher value-added global supply chains.
insights.speaker: HOMI KHARAS
insights.so_what: A potential 7x growth market in regenerative bio-based products is an investment theme to track.
insights.quote: worth about $4 trillion today; unlocking its potential could boost its value to $30 trillion by 2050
insights.locator: A far better approach is to emphasize

insights.claim: Framing conservation as a cost that rich countries foist on poor ones leads credit-rating agencies to downgrade developing countries over slower growth risk; reframing nature protection as a bioeconomy growth strategy is the authors' proposed fix.
insights.speaker: HOMI KHARAS
insights.so_what: Changes in how ratings agencies treat nature could shift sovereign spreads for resource-rich EMs.
insights.locator: The issue is bigger than market failures

insights.claim: Underinvestment in nature is most acute in resource-rich, fiscally constrained countries such as Indonesia, Brazil, Peru, Zambia, Ecuador, the Philippines and Mozambique, which rely on logging, mining and plantation agriculture to earn foreign exchange for external debt service.
insights.speaker: HOMI KHARAS
insights.so_what: Debt pressure drives extraction in these sovereigns—watch debt-for-nature swaps and resilience-linked instruments.
insights.locator: The problem of underinvestment is most acute

insights.claim: Ecological damage from extraction leaves these countries more exposed to floods, droughts and storms that usually trigger rating downgrades, while debt frameworks fail to credit the benefits of building resilience—a self-reinforcing trap.
insights.speaker: HOMI KHARAS
insights.so_what: Sovereign credit analysis may be mispricing climate-resilience investment in EM issuers.
insights.quote: debt frameworks do not properly account for the benefits of building resilience to such shocks
insights.locator: The problem of underinvestment is most acute

insights.claim: Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana produce nearly two-thirds of the world's cocoa, almost entirely on small farms, yet 73–90% of cocoa-producing households there earn little income from it.
insights.speaker: HOMI KHARAS
insights.so_what: Smallholder poverty underpins cocoa supply fragility and price volatility.
insights.quote: Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana produce nearly two-thirds of the world’s cocoa supply

insights.claim: Cocoa smallholders who cannot afford fertilizer and weed-control costs to replant aging trees push into forests where planting new trees is cheaper, driving deforestation.
insights.speaker: HOMI KHARAS
insights.so_what: Aging tree stock and underinvestment constrain cocoa supply and link it to deforestation compliance risk.
insights.locator: Creating the right incentives is especially

insights.claim: The EU, which imports about 58% of the world's cocoa beans, will start applying its Deforestation Regulation to large operators in December 2026, conditioning market access for cocoa, coffee and other commodities on deforestation-free supply chains.
insights.speaker: HOMI KHARAS
insights.so_what: EUDR enforcement from December is a near-term compliance cost and potential supply disruption for cocoa and coffee traders.
insights.quote: The European Union, which imports about 58% of the world’s cocoa beans, will begin to apply the Deforestation Regulation to large operators starting in December

insights.claim: Because chocolate trading, processing and manufacturing are concentrated in a handful of firms, the authors propose big traders finance replanting and traceability so smallholders can comply with the EU rules and earn more.
insights.speaker: HOMI KHARAS
insights.so_what: Large cocoa traders may face pressure to fund supply-chain investments, affecting margins but securing supply.

insights.claim: Environmental crime—illegal logging, mining, wildlife trafficking and fishing—generates an estimated $110–280 billion a year, much laundered through the same channels as narcotics and illicit finance.
insights.speaker: HOMI KHARAS
insights.so_what: AML scrutiny could expand to nature-linked commodity flows, touching banks, traders and ports.
insights.quote: generating an estimated $110–280 billion per year
insights.locator: Protecting nature is also a security imperative

insights.claim: The authors argue enforcement and asset recovery should target chokepoints such as mills, refineries, ports, traders and financiers rather than individual loggers, while securing land rights and finance for Indigenous peoples and local communities.
insights.speaker: HOMI KHARAS
insights.so_what: Intermediaries in commodity chains (refiners, ports, financiers) face rising enforcement exposure.
insights.quote: enforcement and asset recovery should target chokepoints like mills, refineries, ports, traders, and financiers
insights.locator: Protecting nature is also a security imperative

insights.claim: The authors say climate and nature action will be renegotiated at COP31 in Antalya in November 2026 and in UN talks on the post-2030 agenda replacing the Sustainable Development Goals, and urge a focus on changing incentives rather than adding targets.
insights.speaker: HOMI KHARAS
insights.so_what: Watch COP31 outcomes for nature-finance and subsidy-reform commitments.
insights.quote: That means framing nature as an investment, not a cost—and rewarding, not punishing, those who protect it.
insights.locator: The lesson of the State of Biodiversity Action
